## Meridian Freight went from six-week releases to about nine a day

Meridian Freight's platform team used to ship on a six-week cycle. Each release bundled roughly forty merged branches, which made failures expensive to diagnose: when the January release took checkout down for two hours, the on-call engineer spent most of a day bisecting to find the one commit responsible.

"We weren't slow because people wrote code slowly," says Priya Ramanathan, who runs the team. "We were slow because nobody wanted to be the person who broke the release. So everyone waited."

They moved to [Platform] in March, starting with two services rather than the whole estate. The first change was mechanical — every merge to main now builds, runs the test suite, and deploys to staging without anyone asking it to. The second change took longer: the team had to write enough integration coverage that they trusted the pipeline's verdict. That work took about ten weeks.

Production deploys now average nine a day across fourteen services. Change failure rate went from 18% to 4%, and median time to restore dropped from four hours to eleven minutes, mostly because a bad deploy is now one commit instead of forty.

The team kept manual approval on two services that touch customer billing. Ramanathan says that's deliberate and probably permanent.

"The thing I didn't expect was how it changed what people propose," she says. "When shipping is cheap, someone will try the small idea. Before, it wasn't worth the ceremony."

---
